headline: Tiny snakes escape danger by rolling like wheels

sources.title: These tiny snakes cartwheel to escape danger (Science News)
These Snakes Can Cartwheel Away From Danger. Scientists Just Uncovered How the Slithering Creatures Perform Their Acrobatic Rolls (Smithsonian Magazine)
This snake cartwheels to escape danger (Popular Science)

chunks.text: Dwarf reed snakes, tiny snakes from Southeast Asia, have a surprising way to {{get away}} from danger. When they feel [[threatened]], they {{curl up}} and roll along the ground like a wheel. Rolling lets them move about four times faster than they can [[slither]]. This strange [[behavior]] was first [[caught on camera]] in 2019, on a road in Malaysia. Since then, scientists have [[wondered]] how such small animals {{pull it off}}.

chunks.text: A new study {{came out}} on October 19, 2026, in the [[journal]] Current Biology. Its leader, a scientist at Toho University in Japan, wanted to {{figure out}} how the snakes roll. First, his team had to {{track the snakes down}}. They are only about 4 to 11 inches long, and they usually hide under [[dead leaves]].

chunks.text: The team [[collected]] 13 of these snakes in Malaysia, plus six [[close relatives]] [[for comparison]]. In the lab, they {{put together}} a [[racetrack]] about seven feet long, with cameras. Each snake got a [[gentle tap]] to make it move. All 13 snakes {{took off}} down the track in a series of [[cartwheels]]. Their [[top speeds]] were about 4 to 8 miles per hour. None of the relatives rolled.

chunks.text: The videos show each roll [[step by step]]. For a moment, the snake is in the air. Then its tail swings past its head and [[hits the ground]]. The snake keeps its head fairly [[steady]]. A Brown University biologist not involved in the study says rolling probably takes a lot of [[effort]]. Researchers are not sure how long the snakes can {{keep it up}}. In the 1800s, writers told stories about "hoop snakes" that rolled like wheels. The Brown biologist always thought they had {{made them up}}. Now it {{turns out}} a real snake does something similar.

mainIdea.s: Scientists filmed tiny Asian snakes in a lab to show how they roll like wheels. The snakes swing their tails over their heads, which helps them escape danger faster than slithering.
mainIdea.why: The study shows how the snakes curl up and roll. Rolling helps them get away about four times faster than when they slither.

mainIdea.s: A lab study found that these small snakes and their close relatives can all cartwheel when touched. Every animal tested on the track left at high speed in a long series of rolls.
mainIdea.why: Close, but only the 13 snakes from the rolling group took off in cartwheels. The six close relatives did not roll and simply slithered.

mainIdea.s: A team in Malaysia counted the snakes living in one national park and found far fewer than before. Experts warn that the loss of forests now puts several small species at serious risk.
mainIdea.why: The real study is about how tiny snakes pull off their rolls. Researchers filmed them on a racetrack in a lab.

tf.s: When dwarf reed snakes feel threatened, they curl up and roll like a wheel.
tf.why: These snakes curl up and roll along the ground to escape danger.

tf.s: The snakes move more slowly when they roll than when they slither.
tf.why: Rolling helps them get away fast. They move about four times faster than when they slither.

tf.s: A new study shows how the tiny snakes pull off their rolls.
tf.why: The study's videos show each roll step by step, and the snake keeps its head fairly steady.

tf.s: The six close relatives also took off down the track in cartwheels.
tf.why: None of the close relatives rolled. Only the 13 snakes from the rolling group took off in cartwheels.

tf.s: The snakes keep their heads fairly steady as they pull off each roll.
tf.why: Their tails swing past their heads, but their heads stay fairly steady the whole time.

tf.s: Scientists know exactly how long the snakes can keep up their rolling.
tf.why: Researchers are not sure how long the snakes can keep it up, and rolling probably takes a lot of effort.

lines.text: Did you see the video of the snakes that roll like wheels?
No. I'm [[not a fan]] of snakes, but tell me more.
They're called dwarf reed snakes, and they live in Southeast Asia. When they feel threatened, they {{curl up}} and start rolling.
To {{get away}} from danger. They move about four times faster than when they slither.
Right. A new study {{came out}} in October that shows how they do it.
How did scientists even find them?
It wasn't easy to {{track them down}}. They're less than a foot long, and they hide under dead leaves.
Yes. The team {{put together}} a little racetrack with cameras and gave each snake a gentle tap.
All 13 of them. Each roll is over so fast. [[Blink and you'll miss it]].
Can they roll for a long time?
Nobody knows how long they can {{keep it up}}. It probably takes a lot of effort.
My grandpa used to tell a [[tall tale]] about a snake that rolled like a hoop.
People wrote about hoop snakes in the 1800s. A biologist at Brown University thought people {{made them up}}, but it {{turns out}} a real snake does roll.
Well, I'll [[take your word for it]]. I'm still not watching that video.
